overview: Melanoma is the most serious form of skin cancer. It develops in melanocytes (pigment-producing cells) and can spread to other organs if not detected early.
symptoms: Asymmetric shape, irregular borders, multiple colors, diameter >6mm, evolving/changing lesion. May itch, bleed, or crust.
abcde_guidance: Apply ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6mm, Evolution (change over time). Any one sign warrants evaluation.
when_to_see_doctor: Immediately if: changing mole, bleeding, rapid growth, or multiple ABCDE signs. Within 1-2 weeks for any suspicious lesion.
treatment: Surgical excision is primary treatment. Advanced cases may need immunotherapy, targeted therapy, or chemotherapy. Early detection has excellent prognosis.
prevention: Daily SPF 30+ sunscreen, avoid tanning beds, monthly self skin exams, annual dermatologist check (more often if high risk).
risk_factors: Fair skin, many moles, family history of melanoma, history of sunburns, UV exposure, weakened immune system.

overview: A melanocytic nevus (mole) is a common benign growth of pigment cells. Most moles are harmless but should be monitored for changes.
symptoms: Round/oval, uniform color (brown/tan), smooth borders, usually <6mm, stable over time.
abcde_guidance: Monitor with ABCDE. A stable symmetric mole with uniform color is typically benign. Report any evolution.
when_to_see_doctor: If a mole changes in size, shape, color, or begins to itch/bleed. Annual skin check if you have many moles.
treatment: Benign moles usually need no treatment. Suspicious moles are biopsied or removed surgically.
prevention: Sun protection, avoid excessive UV, photograph moles periodically to detect changes.
risk_factors: Multiple atypical moles, fair skin, family history of melanoma.

overview: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. It grows slowly and rarely spreads but can cause local tissue damage if untreated.
symptoms: Pearly or waxy bump, flat flesh-colored lesion, bleeding sore that doesn't heal, pink/red patch, rolled border.
abcde_guidance: BCC often appears as a pearly nodule or non-healing sore rather than a classic dark mole.
when_to_see_doctor: Non-healing sore >3 weeks, bleeding lesion, new growth that ulcerates. See dermatologist within 2-4 weeks.
treatment: Surgical excision, Mohs surgery, cryotherapy, topical treatments depending on type and location.
prevention: Sun protection, avoid tanning, regular skin checks especially for fair-skinned individuals.
risk_factors: Chronic sun exposure, fair skin, age >50, radiation exposure, immunosuppression.

overview: Actinic keratosis (AK) is a precancerous lesion caused by chronic sun damage. Some AKs can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
symptoms: Rough, scaly patch on sun-exposed skin (face, ears, scalp, hands). May be red, pink, or skin-colored. Can feel like sandpaper.
abcde_guidance: AK is a precancerous warning sign, not melanoma. Monitor for thickening, tenderness, or growth.
when_to_see_doctor: If lesion becomes tender, grows, bleeds, or fails to respond to treatment. Prompt dermatology visit.
treatment: Cryotherapy, topical fluorouracil, imiquimod, photodynamic therapy, or curettage.
prevention: Strict sun protection, SPF 30+, protective clothing, regular dermatology follow-up.
risk_factors: Fair skin, age >40, outdoor occupation, history of sunburns, immunosuppression.

overview: Benign keratosis (seborrheic keratosis) is a common harmless waxy growth that appears with age. It is NOT cancerous.
symptoms: Waxy, stuck-on appearance, brown/black/tan color, well-defined borders, may look like it was pasted on skin.
abcde_guidance: Distinct from melanoma: has a 'stuck-on' waxy look with well-defined borders. Still worth confirming with a doctor if unsure.
when_to_see_doctor: If diagnosis is uncertain, lesion irritates, or rapid change occurs.
treatment: Usually no treatment needed. Can be removed if irritated or for cosmetic reasons (cryotherapy, curettage).
prevention: No prevention needed; benign age-related growth. Sun protection still recommended generally.
risk_factors: Age >50, family history of seborrheic keratoses.

overview: Dermatofibroma is a common benign fibrous nodule, usually on the legs. It is harmless and often requires no treatment.
symptoms: Firm, small brownish bump, dimples inward when pinched (dimple sign), usually on lower legs.
abcde_guidance: Benign fibrous nodule — firm and may dimple when squeezed. Not a cancer concern unless diagnosis is uncertain.
when_to_see_doctor: If growing rapidly, painful, or diagnosis uncertain.
treatment: Usually observation only. Surgical removal if symptomatic.
risk_factors: More common in women, often after minor skin injury.

overview: Vascular lesions include hemangiomas and angiomas — benign blood vessel growths on the skin.
symptoms: Red/purple flat or raised spots, blanch with pressure, cherry angioma (bright red dome).
abcde_guidance: Red/purple color that blanches with pressure suggests vascular origin, not melanoma.
when_to_see_doctor: If bleeding frequently, growing rapidly, or diagnosis uncertain.
treatment: Usually no treatment. Laser therapy or excision if needed.
